concept: Write amplification and cache cost of unused indexes

claims.text: A zero $indexStats access count is not a measurement of maintenance work or proof that an index has no value: Percona notes that uniqueness enforcement does not increment the access counter and warns about indexes needed by occasional reporting workloads. (medium confidence)

Before deciding an index is unnecessary, observe a representative application cycle and consider rare but important query patterns. Percona warns about monthly reports; Alibaba illustrates a rarely used leaderboard index that must remain. (medium confidence)

Index maintenance can create cache pressure: MongoDB documents that sufficiently scattered random index inserts can cause high WiredTiger eviction and replacement, requiring disk updates. An index's lack of query reads does not eliminate this write-side access. (medium confidence)

Representative workload coverage matters before removal: Percona warns that an index used only for monthly reporting may appear unused during a shorter observation period, and that retained monitoring history should cover the full application cycle. (low confidence)

Hiding an index removes it from query planning but continues its write maintenance and memory/disk consumption. A hide experiment can assess query dependence, but cannot measure the maintenance savings of actually dropping the index. (medium confidence)

Maintaining unnecessary indexes adds work to writes and consumes storage; removing indexes that the workload does not need can improve write performance and reduce storage requirements. (high confidence)

MongoDB inserts or removes corresponding keys on inserts and deletes. Updates may change only a subset of indexes, depending on affected keys; sparse and partial indexes are maintained only for documents included in them. The blanket statement that every update rewrites every index is too broad. (medium confidence)

Indexes without query benefits can still increase WiredTiger cache pressure through maintenance. Percona describes additional cache evictions and slower operation under over-indexing; Netdata independently identifies unused indexes as a source of cache waste and write amplification. (medium confidence)

WiredTiger uses both an internal cache and the filesystem cache. Indexes in the internal cache have a different representation from their on-disk form and may retain prefix compression; therefore, on-disk index size alone does not establish how much RAM dropping an index will release. (low confidence)

A zero $indexStats access count does not quantify index maintenance cost or prove the absence of useful behavior: the counter covers user-driven access, excludes internal operations such as TTL expiration, and uniqueness checks can occur without incrementing it. (medium confidence)

Alibaba documents another overhead at high object counts: each index adds a disk file and corresponding WiredTiger dhandle structures. Reducing unnecessary indexes reduces those resources; the performance effect depends on workload and access patterns. (low confidence)

No universal RAM or write-latency saving follows from an unused-index count. Percona explicitly scopes its customer example to that workload, while MongoDB describes per-index overhead without a fixed multiplier. Treat estimated benefits as hypotheses for a measured removal experiment. (medium confidence)

Unused indexes can add write work despite serving no queries: MongoDB maintains applicable index entries on inserts and deletes, and Percona identifies excess indexes as overhead on writes, disk and memory. (medium confidence)

The FAST 2022 paper measures physical write amplification as post-compression bytes written to NAND divided by bytes written into the database. Its WiredTiger/B+-tree comparisons vary workload and storage parameters; they do not measure savings from removing unused MongoDB secondary indexes and should not supply a universal index-removal multiplier. (low confidence)
